literal: Those who separated life from the body, they say, are those who have a life of unending misery with a diseased body.
translation: Wise people say that those who live a life of unending misery in a diseased and suffering body are those who once separated life from another's body.
modern: உடம்பிலிருந்து உயிரைப் பிரித்தவர்கள் (கொலை செய்தவர்கள்) என்று, நோயால் துன்புறும் உடம்போடு நீங்காத துன்ப வாழ்க்கையை வாழ்பவர்களை அறிவுடையோர் கூறுவர்.
explanation: This couplet links the act of killing to the physical suffering experienced in a subsequent existence. The poet suggests that those who suffer from chronic, painful diseases and live a life of unending misery (cellā tī vāḻkkai) in a defective body (ceyiṟ uṭampu) are reaping the consequences of having taken another life. The word 'ceyiṟ' means defect or disease, highlighting physical suffering, while 'cellā tī' represents unceasing, fire-like misery. Through this, the chapter on non-killing (kollāmai) emphasizes that the violence inflicted on others ultimately returns to the perpetrator as physical and mental torment.
